lead: This unit turns Coulomb's law and the laws of current into fields, then into four equations that predict light. After it you can find a field with Gauss's law, get a potential, size a capacitor or an inductor, and write down a plane electromagnetic wave with its intensity. It is the unit where electricity, magnetism and optics become one subject.
about: The unit builds the field picture of electricity and magnetism and ends with Maxwell's four equations and the electromagnetic wave. Chapter 3.1 supplies the vector tools — gradient, divergence, curl — and the two integral theorems. Chapters 3.2 and 3.3 find the electric field of charges, first by adding Coulomb forces, then by using Gauss's law. Chapter 3.4 turns the field into a scalar potential and gives Poisson's and Laplace's equations. Chapter 3.5 puts a dielectric between capacitor plates and shows how polarization changes capacitance. Chapters 3.6 and 3.7 repeat the story for currents: Biot–Savart and Ampere's law, then Faraday's law and inductance. Chapter 3.8 assembles Maxwell's equations with boundary conditions, and 3.9 solves them in free space to get plane waves and the Poynting vector.

chapters.idea: Vector calculus turns a field into local numbers — slope, source strength, circulation — and two theorems connect those numbers to integrals over lines, surfaces and volumes.
chapters.depth: Scalar and vector fields; the del operator ∇; gradient of a scalar (direction of steepest rise, magnitude of that rise); divergence of a vector (net outflow per unit volume); curl (circulation per unit area, right-hand rule); the Laplacian ∇². Line, surface and volume integrals, with dS for a surface and dτ for a volume. Divergence theorem ∮F·dS = ∫(∇·F)dτ and Stokes' theorem ∮F·dl = ∫(∇×F)·dS, each stated with the meaning of every symbol. Identities ∇×(∇φ) = 0 and ∇·(∇×F) = 0, used later for conservative fields. One line on the Dirac delta function, ρ = q δ³(r), as a bookkeeping device for a point charge — only a few universities teach this. Some syllabi call the divergence theorem Gauss's theorem and Stokes' theorem the curl theorem.

figure.aria: The del operator splits into four tools: gradient, divergence, curl and the Laplacian, each acting on a different kind of field.

chapters.example: For φ = x²yz and F = (x²y, yz, xz), find ∇φ, ∇·F and ∇×F at the point (1, 2, 3). Answers: ∇φ = (2xyz, x²z, x²y) = (12, 3, 2); ∇·F = 2xy + z + x = 8; ∇×F = (−z, −z, −x²) = (−3, −3, −1).
chapters.trap: Mixing the outputs: divergence gives a scalar, curl gives a vector. Also watch the sign and order in the curl determinant, and never apply the divergence theorem to an open surface — the surface must be closed, with the normal pointing outward.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 vector algebra, and partial derivatives from the first-semester mathematics course.
chapters.leave: The physical use of these tools — electrostatics, magnetostatics, the wave equation — belongs to the later chapters. Detailed delta-function algebra is outside this unit.

chapters.idea: Two point charges push or pull along the line joining them with a force set by q₁q₂/r², and every electric field is that law added up over all the charges.
chapters.depth: Coulomb's law in words and in vector form, with 1/(4πε₀) = 9×10⁹ N m² C⁻² and ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻². Superposition for many charges. Electric field as force per unit test charge, E = F/q₀; field of a point charge; field lines. Short treatment of the dipole field on the axis and on the equator. Continuous distributions: line λ (C/m), surface σ (C/m²), volume ρ (C/m³), each with the field written as an integral. Mention in one line that a point charge can be written as ρ = q δ³(r).

figure.title: From Coulomb to a field
figure.aria: Pair forces are added as vectors, turned into an integral for a continuous distribution, and read as a field at each point.

chapters.example: A charge q₁ = 4 μC sits at the origin and q₂ = −3 μC sits at (0.20 m, 0). Find the force between them and the field at the position of q₂ due to q₁. Force magnitude = 9×10⁹ × (4×10⁻⁶ × 3×10⁻⁶)/0.20² = 2.7 N, attractive, so q₂ is pulled toward the origin. Field due to q₁ at that point = 9×10⁹ × 4×10⁻⁶/0.04 = 9×10⁵ N/C along +x; then q₂E = −3×10⁻⁶ × 9×10⁵ = −2.7 N, the same answer.
chapters.trap: Adding magnitudes instead of adding forces as vectors, and using r in centimetres while k is in SI units. Also μC is 10⁻⁶ C, not 10⁻³ C.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 for the gradient and for integrals of vector fields; Unit 1 for vector addition.
chapters.leave: Symmetric charge distributions are handled in Chapter 3.3 by Gauss's law rather than by integration. Energy of the arrangement comes in Chapter 3.4.

chapters.idea: The total electric flux out of any closed surface depends only on the charge inside it, so a well-chosen surface replaces a hard integral by one multiplication.
chapters.depth: Flux Φ = ∮E·dS with dS outward. Statement of Gauss's law, integral form ∮E·dS = Q_enclosed/ε₀ and differential form ∇·E = ρ/ε₀. Applications worked fully: infinite line charge (E = λ/2πε₀r), infinite sheet (E = σ/2ε₀), spherical shell (zero inside, kQ/r² outside), uniformly charged solid sphere, and a charged conductor (field inside zero, all charge on the outer surface). Note that this is one of Maxwell's four equations and appears again in Chapter 3.8.

figure.aria: The outer box holds every charge in space; only the charges inside the inner box fix the net flux through the closed surface.

chapters.example: An infinite line carries λ = 5 μC/m. Find E at r = 10 cm from it. Take a cylinder of radius r and length L as the Gaussian surface: flux = E × 2πrL, enclosed charge = λL, so E = λ/(2πε₀r) = 9×10⁵ N/C, pointing radially away from the line.
chapters.trap: Putting the total charge of the problem into Q_enclosed. A charge outside the surface gives zero net flux but still adds to E at every point on the surface, so 'flux zero' never means 'field zero'.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.1 and 3.2: surface integrals, the divergence theorem, and the field of a point charge.
chapters.leave: The potential of these same distributions is Chapter 3.4. Flux through open surfaces and magnetic flux wait for Chapter 3.7.

chapters.idea: Potential is the work per unit charge needed to bring a charge in from infinity, a scalar that stores the whole field in one number, and where charge sits, Poisson's equation fixes its second derivatives.
chapters.depth: Definition V = −∫E·dl from a reference point, and E = −∇V as the inverse relation. Potential of a point charge kQ/r, of a dipole, equipotential surfaces, and why conductors are equipotentials. Potential energy of a system: W = ½ΣqᵢVᵢ, W = ½∫ρV dτ, W = ½ε₀∫E² dτ, with the energy density ½ε₀E². Poisson's equation ∇²V = −ρ/ε₀ and Laplace's equation ∇²V = 0 where there is no charge. Boundary condition: V is continuous. One solved case of Laplace between two plates (linear V) and around a conducting sphere. Method of images and multipole expansion: only a few universities teach these — one paragraph each, no long derivation.

figure.aria: Potential falls as 1/r and the field as 1/r²; the field curve is the steeper one and both blow up at the charge.

chapters.example: The potential in a region is V = x²y + yz volts, with x, y, z in metres. Find E and the charge density at (1, 2, 3). E = −∇V = −(2xy, x² + z, y) = (−4, −4, −2) V/m. Also ∇²V = 2y = 4 m⁻², so by Poisson's equation ρ = −ε₀∇²V = −8.854×10⁻¹² × 4 = −3.54×10⁻¹¹ C/m³.
chapters.trap: Dropping the minus sign in E = −∇V, and using Laplace's equation in a region that contains charge. Laplace holds only where ρ = 0; with charge present you must use Poisson.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.1 to 3.3: gradient, the field of a charge, and Gauss's law for symmetric cases.
chapters.leave: Capacitance and stored energy in a real device are Chapter 3.5. Image charges and multipoles are named here and not developed.

chapters.idea: A dielectric has no free charge to give; its molecules stretch into dipoles, and that polarization weakens the field inside, which the vector D keeps tidy.
chapters.depth: Polar and nonpolar molecules, induced dipoles, alignment. Polarization P = dipole moment per unit volume (C/m²); bound surface charge σ_b = P·n̂ and bound volume charge ρ_b = −∇·P. Electric displacement D = ε₀E + P, Gauss's law in dielectrics ∇·D = ρ_free. Susceptibility P = ε₀χ_eE, relative permittivity ε_r = 1 + χ_e, dielectric constant K = ε_r; typical values (air ≈ 1, mica ≈ 6, water ≈ 80). Dielectric strength and breakdown. Capacitors: C = ε₀ε_rA/d for a parallel plate, series and parallel combinations, energy ½CV² = Q²/2C, energy density ½ε₀ε_rE². Compare battery connected and battery removed on inserting the slab.

figure.title: What a dielectric does
figure.aria: Free charge on the plates lines up molecular dipoles, which leave bound charge on the faces and raise the capacitance by the factor ε_r.

chapters.example: A parallel plate capacitor has plate area A = 0.02 m², separation d = 1 mm, and mica of ε_r = 5 fills the gap. The battery keeps V = 100 V. Find C₀, C, Q, the field and the stored energy. C₀ = ε₀A/d = 8.854×10⁻¹² × 0.02/0.001 = 177 pF. With mica C = 5 × 177 = 885 pF. Q = CV = 885×10⁻¹² × 100 = 8.85×10⁻⁸ C. E = V/d = 100/0.001 = 1×10⁵ V/m. Energy = ½CV² = 4.43×10⁻⁶ J.
chapters.trap: Forgetting which quantity is held fixed. With the battery connected, V and E stay and Q grows by ε_r; with the battery removed, Q stays and E falls to E₀/ε_r.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.4 for potential and stored energy, and Chapter 3.3 for Gauss's law with free charge.
chapters.leave: Ferroelectric and piezoelectric behaviour belongs elsewhere; ionic conduction in dielectrics is not needed here.

chapters.idea: A steady current sets up a magnetic field whose direction follows the right-hand rule, and for symmetric currents Ampere's law reduces the field to one line of arithmetic.
chapters.depth: Current element Idl and the Biot–Savart law dB = (μ₀/4π) I dl × r̂/r², with μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹. Field of a long straight wire, at the centre of a circular loop and on its axis, of a solenoid (B = μ₀nI) and a toroid. Ampere's law ∮B·dl = μ₀I_enclosed and its differential form ∇×B = μ₀J. Vector potential A with B = ∇×A: only a few universities teach this — one paragraph. Magnetic materials in brief: magnetization M, H = B/μ₀ − M, μ_r, and one line that dia, para and ferromagnetism with hysteresis are studied in Unit 7.

figure.aria: The field of a long straight wire falls as 1/r, while the field on the axis of a loop falls much faster, as 1/r³ far away.

chapters.example: A long straight wire and a circular loop of radius 5 cm both carry 2 A. Find B at 10 cm from the wire and B at the centre of the loop. Wire: B = μ₀I/2πr = (4π×10⁻⁷ × 2)/(2π × 0.1) = 4×10⁻⁶ T = 4 μT. Loop centre: B = μ₀I/2R = (4π×10⁻⁷ × 2)/(2 × 0.05) = 2.5×10⁻⁵ T = 25 μT.
chapters.trap: Direction mistakes in dl × r̂, and using the total current instead of the enclosed current in Ampere's law. The simple form of Ampere's law also needs steady currents and high symmetry.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 for curl and Stokes' theorem, and Chapter 3.5 for the D, P, χ_e pattern that M, H, μ_r repeats.
chapters.leave: Dia, para and ferromagnetic behaviour, domains and hysteresis are Unit 7. Time-varying currents are Chapter 3.7.

chapters.idea: A changing magnetic flux pushes charges around a loop, and a loop resists any change in its own current — two views of one law.
chapters.depth: Magnetic flux Φ = ∫B·dS (weber). Faraday's law ε = −dΦ/dt in words, in integral form ∮E·dl = −dΦ/dt, and in differential form ∇×E = −∂B/∂t. Lenz's law as the meaning of the minus sign. Motional emf ε = Blv for a rod moving in a field, with the three directions mutually perpendicular; eddy currents in one paragraph. Self-inductance L = Φ/I, mutual inductance, L of a solenoid μ₀n²Al, energy in an inductor ½LI² and magnetic energy density B²/2μ₀. LR circuit: i = (ε/R)(1 − e^{−Rt/L}), time constant L/R, and decay e^{−Rt/L}.

figure.aria: In an LR circuit the current climbs to its final value with time constant L/R and, once the source is removed, decays along the mirrored curve.

chapters.example: A rod of length 0.2 m slides at 3 m/s on rails in a uniform field B = 0.5 T, with the circuit resistance 1.5 Ω. Find the emf, current, force needed and power. ε = Blv = 0.5 × 0.2 × 3 = 0.3 V; I = ε/R = 0.2 A; force F = BIl = 0.5 × 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.02 N; power in the resistor I²R = 0.06 W, equal to the mechanical power Fv = 0.02 × 3 = 0.06 W.
chapters.trap: Getting Lenz's law backwards: the induced current opposes the change in flux, not the flux itself. Also a rod moving parallel to B has zero motional emf, and L depends on geometry, never on the current.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.6 and 3.1: magnetic field of currents, and curl with Stokes' theorem.
chapters.leave: Mutual inductance between coils in a transformer and AC circuit theory are outside this unit.

chapters.idea: Four equations — Gauss for E, Gauss for B, Faraday, Ampere–Maxwell — hold every classical electric and magnetic fact, once Ampere's law gains the displacement-current term.
chapters.depth: The trouble with Ampere's law at a charging capacitor: continuity of current fails unless a displacement current I_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt is added. The four equations in both integral and differential form, with names: ∇·D = ρ_free, ∇·B = 0, ∇×E = −∂B/∂t, ∇×H = J + ∂D/∂t. Constitutive relations D = ε₀ε_rE, B = μ₀μ_rH, J = σE, and the continuity equation ∇·J = −∂ρ/∂t. Boundary conditions: E_t continuous, D_n jumps by free surface charge σ_f, B_n continuous, H_t jumps by surface current K. One paragraph on significance: unification of electricity, magnetism and optics.

figure.title: Four equations, one wave
figure.aria: The two Gauss laws, Faraday's law and the Ampere–Maxwell law are the complete set, and in free space they combine into a wave equation.

chapters.example: A 1 nF capacitor is charged so that its voltage rises at dV/dt = 10⁶ V/s. Find the displacement current in the gap and its density if the plates have area 0.01 m². I_d = C dV/dt = 1×10⁻⁹ × 10⁶ = 1×10⁻³ A = 1 mA, the same as the conduction current in the wire. J_d = I_d/A = 1×10⁻³/0.01 = 0.1 A/m².
chapters.trap: Applying Ampere's law to a capacitor circuit without the displacement term, and swapping which component is continuous at a boundary: E tangential is continuous while D normal jumps by σ_f.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.3, 3.5, 3.6 and 3.7: Gauss's law, D and P, Ampere's law, and Faraday's law.
chapters.leave: The wave equation that follows from these equations is Chapter 3.9; reflection of light at surfaces is treated in Unit 4.

chapters.idea: In empty space Maxwell's equations admit travelling waves in which E and B oscillate in phase, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel, and carry energy given by the Poynting vector.
chapters.depth: Combining ∇×E = −∂B/∂t with ∇×H = ∂D/∂t gives ∇²E = μ₀ε₀ ∂²E/∂t². Identify c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) = 3×10⁸ m/s, and v = 1/√(με) = c/n in a medium. Transverse nature, the ratio E/B = c, plane wave E = E₀ sin(kz − ωt) with ω = ck, and the right-handed set E, B, k. Energy density u = ½ε₀E₀², Poynting vector S = E×H (W/m²), average intensity ½ε₀cE₀², momentum and radiation pressure. Production by an oscillating dipole antenna and reception by a phone antenna (Syllabus A's cell-phone reception), in a short physical description. One line that reflection and refraction follow from the boundary conditions of Chapter 3.8 and are worked out in Unit 4.

figure.aria: E and B rise and fall together along the direction of travel; B is drawn at half height only so both curves can be seen.

chapters.example: A plane wave in free space has peak electric field E₀ = 30 V/m. Find B₀, the average intensity and the average energy density. B₀ = E₀/c = 30/(3×10⁸) = 1×10⁻⁷ T. Intensity I = ½ε₀cE₀² = 0.5 × 8.854×10⁻¹² × 3×10⁸ × 900 = 1.2 W/m². Energy density u = ½ε₀E₀² = 0.5 × 8.854×10⁻¹² × 900 = 3.98×10⁻⁹ J/m³, and u × c gives back the same intensity.
chapters.trap: Writing B₀ = cE₀ instead of E₀/c, and using E₀² rather than ½E₀² for the average. E and B are in phase in a plane wave, so both peak together.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.8 for Maxwell's equations, Chapter 3.7 for Faraday's law, and Unit 2 for the idea of a wave equation.
chapters.leave: Interference, diffraction, thin films and polarisation of light are Unit 4. Antenna design and communication electronics are outside this book.
